title: Primary school students’ perceptions of artificial intelligence – for good or bad
venue: International Journal of Technology and Design Education
extended_summary:
This case study asks how primary school students perceive artificial intelligence (AI), both cognitively and affectively, and whether they already use AI tools in everyday or school-related tasks. It also explores how students understand AI after a short instructional project on AI literacy and related classroom activities.

The intervention was a school-based AI project in a Swedish compulsory primary school. Grade 5–6 students (ages 11–12) took part in ten 40-minute lessons over several weeks, taught by their science and technology teachers using lesson plans on AI. Activities included introductory discussions of AI examples, algorithms and machine learning, ethical dilemmas, and later student use of ChatGPT for test practice; at a university visit, students also used ChatGPT and DALL-E to create stories and hear a short AI lecture. Data came from a pre-test, focus group interviews with 12 students, and 30 short written evaluation reports.

Findings show that students viewed AI as both a machine and a humanlike or brain-like system, often associating it with robots, computers, phones, Google, Snapchat, Tesla, and self-driving cars. Their attitudes were mixed: they appreciated AI’s usefulness for studying and practical tasks, but were also worried about rapid development, job loss, privacy invasion, cheating, and potential harm. Students reported some prior use of AI and, after the project, emphasized the need for regulation and slower, more careful development. The study concludes that even young students already have meaningful AI perceptions and concerns, and that AI literacy education should address both use and ethics.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by primary school students during lessons about AI and for creating practice questions before tests; also discussed as an AI tool students had used or heard about.

findings.finding_summary: This qualitative case study reports that students used ChatGPT for generating practice questions before tests and viewed it as helpful for studies, but also raised concerns about cheating, rapid development, privacy invasion, and potential harm. The paper does not report an experimental effect size for ChatGPT; evidence is based on pre-test responses, focus groups (n=12), and evaluation reports (n=30) from a total sample of 60 students.
findings.measure: Student-reported use, perceived usefulness, and concerns about ChatGPT and other AI tools

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods case study rather than an experimental evaluation, so it provides descriptive evidence but no causal estimate. The study is useful for documenting student perceptions and concerns, but not for strong efficacy claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows practical uptake and perceived usefulness of ChatGPT, but the evidence is not quantitative and includes notable concerns and potential harms. No effect size is reported, so impact is unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.
